ancient_source: Polybius, Histories 3.113.5 (eight legions plus allied contingents, c. 80,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry)
modern_scholar: J. F. Lazenby, Hannibal's War: A Military History of the Second Punic War (University of Oklahoma Press, 1978)
modern_citation: Lazenby, J.F. (1978). Hannibal's War: A Military History of the Second Punic War. Warminster: Aris & Phillips; Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, pp. 74-77.
notes: Canonical faithful anchor per project brief. Polybius' figure for the eight legions raised for the Cannae campaign is treated by modern military historians (Lazenby; also Goldsworthy, Cannae, 2001) as a reasonable approximation of actual strength, unlike his casualty figures for the same battle (see cannae_roman_casualties). Author is Achaean-Greek, embedded with the pro-Scipionic tradition but not Roman himself, hence side_role neutral rather than own_side_of_author.

ancient_source: Polybius, Histories 3.117.2-4 (70,000 killed, c. 10,000 captured, c. 3,000 escaped); Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 22.49 gives a lower c. 47,700 infantry and 2,700 cavalry dead
modern_scholar: Gregory Daly, Cannae: The Experience of Battle in the Second Punic War (Routledge, 2002)
modern_citation: Daly, G. (2002). Cannae: The Experience of Battle in the Second Punic War. London: Routledge, pp. 195-201.
notes: Even Polybius and Livy, both close to the event, disagree with each other by roughly 20,000 (70,000 vs c. 50,200), itself a sign that ancient reporters of their own catastrophic losses were working from round numbers or political motives rather than a muster. Modern historians reconstruct a smaller field army (see cannae_roman_troops) and correspondingly discount the death toll. One of at most three casualty rows in this file.

side_label: Ptolemaic army under Ptolemy IV Philopator
ancient_source: Polybius, Histories 5.65 and 5.79 (70,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry, 73 elephants)
modern_scholar: Bezalel Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army: Organization and Tactics in the Great Campaigns (Cambridge University Press, 1976); Christelle Fischer-Bovet, Army and Society in Ptolemaic Egypt (Cambridge University Press, 2014)
modern_citation: Bar-Kochva, B. (1976). The Seleucid Army: Organization and Tactics in the Great Campaigns. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, ch. 10; Fischer-Bovet, C. (2014). Army and Society in Ptolemaic Egypt. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
notes: Polybius' detailed order of battle (including the novel 20,000-strong native Egyptian phalanx) is thought to derive from a near-contemporary, administratively-grounded source (probably Ptolemy of Megalopolis or the court historian Zeno of Rhodes) rather than rhetorical exaggeration, and is broadly accepted by modern specialists on Hellenistic armies. A minority reading of the manuscript tradition would lower the Ptolemaic infantry to c. 50,000, which would push this case out of the faithful band; the majority reading is used here.

ancient_source: Caesar, Civil War (Bellum Civile) 3.89 (eighty cohorts, amounting to twenty-two thousand men)
modern_scholar: Si Sheppard, Pharsalus 48 BC: Caesar and Pompey - Clash of the Titans (Osprey Campaign 174, 2006)
modern_citation: Sheppard, S. (2006). Pharsalus 48 BC: Caesar and Pompey - Clash of the Titans. Oxford: Osprey Publishing, pp. 39-41.
notes: Caesar is counting his own cohorts, a figure historians generally treat as reliable precisely because it is a self-administrative count of one's own units rather than an estimate of the enemy or of casualties; contrast his much less trusted figure for Pompey's army of 45,000 at 3.88, which is not used here. Cavalry (c. 1,000) is reported separately by Caesar and is not folded into this infantry figure.

ancient_source: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 16.85.5-6 (30,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry)
modern_citation: Hammond, N.G.L. (1994). Philip of Macedon. London: Duckworth, pp. 148-151.
notes: Diodorus' figure for the Macedonian army is generally accepted at face value by modern historians of Philip's reign; it is the Greek allied total, not the Macedonian one, that is more disputed. Diodorus, a first-century BC Sicilian Greek writing a universal history, has no particular partisan stake in either Macedon or the Greek allied cities at Chaeronea, hence side_role neutral. NOTE: an earlier web-search hit for this battle's Wikidata id (Q205887) resolved to 'Battle of Carrhae' and was discarded after live verification; Q200716 was confirmed by fetching Special:EntityData.

ancient_source: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 33.4 (16,000 phalanx, 2,000 peltasts, 2,000 Thracian/Illyrian light troops, 3,500 southern-Greek/Illyrian light infantry, 2,000 cavalry)
modern_scholar: J.D. Morgan, 'The Campaign and Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 B.C.', Journal of Hellenic Studies 101 (1981)
modern_citation: Morgan, J.D. (1981). 'The Campaign and Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 B.C.' Journal of Hellenic Studies, 101, pp. 16-38.
notes: Livy's breakdown of Philip's field army is a detailed unit-by-unit muster rather than a round rhetorical number, and Morgan's philological reconstruction of the campaign follows it closely. Livy, writing Roman history, treats Macedon as the enemy power, hence enemy_of_author, but the figure shows no sign of the inflation seen in the Persian-war material below. Distinct from the unrelated 364 BC Battle of Cynoscephalae (Q2334746), which was ruled out during Wikidata verification.

ancient_source: Polybius, Histories 3.84.7; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 22.7.2 (both give 15,000 Roman dead)
modern_scholar: Adrian Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage: The Punic Wars 265-146 BC (Cassell, 2000)
modern_citation: Goldsworthy, A. (2000). The Fall of Carthage: The Punic Wars 265-146 BC. London: Cassell, pp. 191-196.
notes: Two independent traditions (Polybius' Greek source and Livy's, ultimately drawing on Fabius Pictor) converge on the same figure for a disaster suffered by the author's own side, which modern historians accept largely unchanged. Included as a faithful casualty anchor, contrasting with the inflated Cannae casualty figure in this file, to show that own-side disaster reports are not automatically inflated. Second and last of the casualty rows in this file (cap is three).

ancient_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.8.6 (1,000,000 infantry, 40,000 cavalry)
modern_scholar: Peter Green, Alexander of Macedon, 356-323 B.C.: A Historical Biography (University of California Press, 1991); John Warry, Warfare in the Classical World (1998)
modern_citation: Green, P. (1991). Alexander of Macedon, 356-323 B.C.: A Historical Biography. Berkeley: University of California Press; Warry, J. (1998). Warfare in the Classical World. Norman: University of Oklahoma Press.
notes: Ancient sources disagree wildly among themselves (Diodorus 800,000 infantry + 200,000 cavalry; Curtius Rufus 200,000 infantry + 45,000 cavalry; Plutarch a round 1,000,000), itself a marker of literary inflation rather than transmitted record-keeping. Arrian, drawing chiefly on Alexander's officer Ptolemy, has every reason to magnify the scale of Alexander's victory over the enemy.

ancient_source: Herodotus, Histories 7.60.1 (land infantry alone; Herodotus separately doubles this for camp followers, and the poet Simonides is elsewhere quoted as claiming four million)
modern_scholar: J.F. Lazenby, The Defence of Greece 480-479 B.C. (Aris & Phillips, 1993)
modern_citation: Lazenby, J.F. (1993). The Defence of Greece 480-479 B.C. Warminster: Aris & Phillips, pp. 90-98.
notes: One of the most extreme inflation ratios in the ancient historiographic record; even among ancient authors, Herodotus was seen as conservative next to Simonides' four million. Hans Delbruck's far lower estimate (15,000-25,000), based on logistics/road-capacity arguments, is a minority position among military historians and is not used for modern_figure here, but is flagged as the low end of the debate.

side_label: Achaemenid Persian force landed at Marathon
ancient_source: Cornelius Nepos, Miltiades 4-5 (200,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry embarked in total; of these, 100,000 infantry landed and fought at Marathon, the rest held back with the fleet)
modern_scholar: Peter Krentz, The Battle of Marathon (Yale University Press, 2010)
modern_citation: Krentz, P. (2010). The Battle of Marathon. New Haven: Yale University Press, pp. 116-145.
notes: Herodotus himself gives no number for the Persian army at Marathon; the explicit figures come from later authors (Nepos, Plutarch, Pausanias, Plato, Justin), rising over time from 200,000 to 600,000, illustrating numbers inflating with narrative distance from the event. Nepos' figure is used here as the earliest of the numbered later sources with a clear locus.

ancient_source: Herodotus, Histories 9.32 (300,000 Persian troops, excluding a further 50,000 Greek allies of Persia counted separately)
modern_scholar: J.F. Lazenby, The Defence of Greece 480-479 B.C. (Aris & Phillips, 1993)
modern_citation: Lazenby, J.F. (1993). The Defence of Greece 480-479 B.C. Warminster: Aris & Phillips, pp. 227-232.
notes: The Greek allies of Persia (a further 50,000 per Herodotus) are excluded from ancient_figure to keep a like-for-like Persian-only comparison; including them would raise the ratio further. Less extreme than the Thermopylae or Marathon ratios, consistent with Plataea being fought a year into the invasion when both sides' real strengths were better known to Greek observers.

side_label: Achaemenid Persian army under Darius III
ancient_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 2.8.8; Plutarch, Alexander 18.4 (both give totals of approximately 600,000)
modern_scholar: Donald Engels, Alexander the Great and the Logistics of the Macedonian Army (University of California Press, 1978); Peter Green, Alexander of Macedon, 356-323 B.C. (University of California Press, 1991)
modern_citation: Engels, D.W. (1978). Alexander the Great and the Logistics of the Macedonian Army. Berkeley: University of California Press; Green, P. (1991). Alexander of Macedon, 356-323 B.C.: A Historical Biography. Berkeley: University of California Press.
notes: Curtius Rufus gives a lower 250,000, and Diodorus/Justin 400,000, but even the lowest ancient figure is far above modern reconstructions. Devine's terrain analysis (the Pinarus/Payas river plain is very narrow) is the main modern argument for a much smaller engaged force; Delbruck's outlier estimate of 25,000 is even lower and is not used for modern_figure here. Note: an initial web-search hit for this battle's Wikidata id (Q2170603) resolved on verification to the unrelated 194 CE Battle of Issus between Severus and Niger and was discarded; Q201526 was confirmed by fetching Special:EntityData.

ancient_source: Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 7.75-76 (contingents from Gallic tribes totalling c. 250,000 infantry and 8,000 cavalry)
modern_scholar: Adrian Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (Yale University Press, 2006); Peter Connolly, Greece and Rome at War (Greenhill Books, rev. 1998)
modern_citation: Goldsworthy, A. (2006). Caesar: Life of a Colossus. New Haven: Yale University Press, pp. 358-361; Connolly, P. (1998). Greece and Rome at War. London: Greenhill Books.
notes: Caesar's own figure for his opponents follows the pattern of enemy-army inflation seen elsewhere in the Commentaries (e.g. the Helvetii, see bibracte_helvetii_troops); it is also his own account, so both enemy_of_author and self-serving political-memoir motives apply. Modern historians accept that the Gauls significantly outnumbered Caesar's roughly 60,000-70,000 besieging/counter-besieging force but reject the ancient total by roughly half or more.

ancient_source: Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.29 (tally from a register in Greek script found in the Helvetii camp: 368,000 persons total, of whom 92,000 were able to bear arms)
modern_scholar: Catherine Gilliver, Caesar's Gallic Wars 58-50 BC (Osprey Essential Histories, 2002)
modern_citation: Gilliver, C. (2002). Caesar's Gallic Wars 58-50 BC. Oxford: Osprey Publishing, pp. 24-27.
notes: Unusually for this file, Caesar's figure is presented as drawn from a captured administrative document (a census-like tally in Greek script) rather than as his own rhetorical claim, which is why ancient_claim_regime is administrative_partisan rather than chronicle; even so, modern historians treat the 92,000 fighting-men figure as inflated, whether by Helvetii record-keeping practice or by Caesar's transmission of it. Delbruck's much lower estimate of c. 12,000 is an outlier not used for modern_figure.

ancient_source: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 37.37; Appian, Syriaca 32 (both give a Seleucid total of approximately 70,000, including 12,000 cavalry, scythed chariots and elephants)
modern_scholar: John D. Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (Brill, 2002)
modern_citation: Grainger, J.D. (2002). The Roman War of Antiochos the Great. Leiden: Brill, pp. 324-330.
notes: Grainger argues the two armies at Magnesia were probably much closer in size than Livy/Appian suggest, with Antiochus fielding closer to 50,000 than 70,000, similar to the Roman-allied total; this sits right at the edge of the faithful band (|log_ratio| just above 0.3) rather than the extreme-inflation range seen in the Persian Wars material.
